power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "P<0.05", Text = "Functional enrichment analysis was performed to characterize biological pathways and processes represented by proteins significantly associated with incident epilepsy in the Cox proportional hazards analyses (Bonferroni-adjusted P<0.05)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. text.text: Epilepsy affects approximately 50 million people worldwide, yet biomarkers capable of identifying individuals at risk before clinical onset are lacking, and the molecular mechanisms preceding disease onset remain poorly understood.
Here, we integrated plasma proteomic, metabolomic, and genomic data from the UK Biobank to characterize molecular changes preceding epilepsy and evaluate their predictive and causal relevance.
We quantified 2,923 plasma proteins in ~53,000 participants and followed incident epilepsy for up to 15 years before epilepsy diagnosis.
Cox proportional hazards analyses identified 116 proteins associated with incident epilepsy, led by neurofilament light chain (NEFL; HR=2.03) and growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15; HR=1.73).
These proteins were enriched for extracellular signaling, immune regulation, and cell-death pathways and displayed distinct subtype-and age-specific signatures.
A proteomic risk score comprising 32 proteins stratified epilepsy risk, with individuals in the highest quintile exhibiting a 3.5-fold greater risk than those in the lowest quintile (AUC=0.70).

In parallel, 154 of 249 circulating metabolites were associated with incident epilepsy, with the strongest inverse association observed for citrate (HR=0.72) and positive associations across HDL-related metabolites (HR=1.16-1.21), implicating dysregulated energy and lipoprotein metabolism.
A metabolomic risk score showed more modest discrimination (AUC=0.63).

Integrating proteomic, metabolomic, polygenic, and demographic information yielded an overall AUC of 0.71 for incident epilepsy; in a separate cross-sectional analysis of individuals with earlyonset epilepsy discrimination reached an AUC of 0.79.
Proteome-wide cis-pQTL Mendelian randomization identified 12 proteins associated with epilepsy after false discovery rate correction, predominantly for genetic generalized epilepsy.
O-GlcNAcase (OGA), a regulator of protein O-GlcNAcylation with established roles in neuronal function and synaptic plasticity, showed the strongest protective association (OR=0.71, FDR=2.7×10 ).
Serine protease 53 (PRSS53), a poorly characterized serine protease, showed strong evidence for a potential shared causal variant with epilepsy (colocalization PP.H4=0.95).

Together, these findings demonstrate that circulating molecular alterations precede epilepsy diagnosis by years and reveal complementary proteomic, metabolic, and genetic determinants of disease susceptibility, providing a framework for biologically informed risk stratification and therapeutic target prioritization.

Epilepsy comprises a heterogeneous group of neurological disorders characterized by a persistent predisposition to generate unprovoked seizures and affects approximately 50 million individuals worldwide, contributing significantly to the global disease burden. 1, 2 Despite major advances in neuroimaging, electrophysiology, and molecular genetics, epilepsy diagnosis remains largely symptom-driven and frequently occurs only after seizure onset.

text.text: Recent advances in high-throughput molecular profiling now enable comprehensive characterization of complementary biological processes before disease onset.

Circulating plasma proteomics reflects immune activation, neuronal injury, extracellular signalling, and tissue-specific responses, whereas plasma metabolomics captures alterations in intermediary metabolism, mitochondrial function, oxidative stress, lipid metabolism, and energy homeostasis. [8] [9] [10] Integrating these complementary molecular layers therefore offers a unique opportunity to characterize systemic biological changes that precede epilepsy development. [11] [12] [13] Large population-based studies have demonstrated that circulating molecular profiles can predict future disease years before clinical diagnosis.

[14] [15] [16] Likewise, metabolomic profiling has revealed predictive signatures across neurological and cardiometabolic disorders, highlighting its ability to capture dynamic biological processes that are not reflected by inherited genetic variation. 17, 18 In epilepsy, perturbations of energy metabolism are biologically plausible because the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle intermediate citrate links mitochondrial function to glutamate and γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) synthesis, while lossof-function variants in the citrate transporter gene SLC13A5 cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE). text.text: Within epilepsy, biomarker research has expanded considerably during recent years.

Circulating neurofilament light chain (NEFL), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), inflammatory mediators, and several metabolic pathways have been associated with seizure burden, neuronal injury, pharmacoresistance, and disease progression. [22] [23] [24] [25] [26] More recently, Zhang et al. demonstrated in a large prospective population-based study that plasma proteomic profiles are associated with incident epilepsy and identified molecular alterations preceding clinical disease onset, highlighting pathways related to immune regulation, inflammation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and cellular stress responses. 27 While these findings established plasma proteomics as a promising approach for epilepsy biomarker discovery, they also raise the question: which circulating molecules merely predict future epilepsy and which are likely to contribute directly to disease pathogenesis.

text.text: Furthermore, the complementary contributions of inherited genetic susceptibility, circulating proteins, and metabolic alterations to epilepsy risk remain largely unexplored.

Human genetics provides an orthogonal perspective on disease biology because germline genetic variants are fixed throughout life and are therefore largely unaffected by disease progression or reverse causation.

Polygenic scores (PRSs) aggregate the effects of thousands of common variants and have emerged as a powerful tool for quantifying genetic liability across complex diseases, including generalized genetic epilepsy (GGE) and focal epilepsy (FE).

However, PRSs capture inherited susceptibility rather than downstream biological processes and their predictive performance depends strongly on phenotype definition, ancestry, and the underlying genetic architecture. [28] [29] [30] [31] Conversely, circulating molecular profiles integrate both inherited and acquired biological processes occurring during disease development.

text.text: Here, we integrated prospective plasma proteomics, metabolomics, PRSs, and proteome-wide MR within the UK Biobank (UKB) to characterize molecular alterations preceding incident epilepsy.

We first identified circulating proteins and metabolites associated with future epilepsy risk, then evaluated their predictive performance individually and in combination with inherited genetic susceptibility, and finally prioritized genetically supported molecular determinants using MR and BC (Figure 1).

The workflow proceeds through two linked stages.

In the association and molecular risk prediction stage, Cox proportional-hazards models tested circulating protein and metabolite levels against incident epilepsy, followed by construction and comparison of proteomic (ProRS), metabolomic (MetRS), and polygenic (PRS) risk scores for predictive performance.

In the genetic causal prioritization stage, cis-pQTLs and metabolite QTLs served as instruments for two-sample Mendelian randomization (Wald ratio, with Steiger filtering and FDR correction), and markers surviving correction were carried forward to Bayesian colocalization and SuSiE-based multi-signal finemapping to confirm a shared causal variant between molecular trait and epilepsy risk.
This staged design allows observational associations to be distinguished from genetically supported causal relationships.
This study utilized data from the UK Biobank (UKB), a prospective population-based cohort of ~500,000 individuals aged 40-69 at recruitment between 2006 and 2010.

Participants underwent extensive baseline phenotyping, including demographic, lifestyle, clinical, genetics, and molecular assessments, and were subsequently followed longitudinally through linked hospital admission records, death registries, and primary care data.
All participants provided written informed consent.

UKB received ethical approval from the North West Multi-centre Research Ethics Committee (MREC) and all analyses were performed under the relevant UKB application in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. 37

text.text: Epilepsy diagnosis was defined using linked hospital records and self-reported medical history.

Cases were defined by the presence of epilepsy diagnosis recorded using ICD-10 codes G40 and G41, ICD-9 code 345, or self-reported epilepsy (UKB Data-Field 20002, code 1264). 38 Generalized genetic epilepsy (GGE) was defined using ICD-10 codes G40.3, G40.4, G40.6, and G40.7 and the corresponding ICD-9 codes 345.0-345.3.

text.text: Focal epilepsy (FE) was defined using ICD-10 codes G40.0, G40.1 and G40.2 with corresponding ICD-9 345.4, 345.5, and 345.7.
Participants without any epilepsy diagnosis recorded at baseline and at any follow-up were classified as controls.
The primary analyses focused on incident epilepsy.
Incident epilepsy cases were defined as participants who received their first recorded epilepsy diagnosis after the baseline blood collection used for plasma proteomic and metabolomic profiling.
Individuals with an epilepsy diagnosis preceding baseline assessment were considered prevalent cases and excluded from the primary analyses.
This study design ensured that circulating molecular profiles preceded clinical disease onset, allowing evaluation of biomarkers associated with future epilepsy risk rather than established disease.

Associations between baseline plasma protein abundance and incident epilepsy were evaluated using Cox proportional hazards regression models, with protein normalized protein expression (NPX) values included as continuous predictors.
Hazard ratios (HRs) and corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated for each protein.

All models were adjusted for age at assessment, sex, body mass index (BMI), smoking status, alcohol consumption, history of stroke, and the first four genetic principal components (PCs) to account for population stratification.
To account for multiple testing across all proteins, statistical significance was determined using Bonferroni correction, with a Bonferroniadjusted P-value < 0.05 considered significant.

text.text: To evaluate whether identified biomarkers were also associated with established disease, we performed secondary logistic regression analyses of prevalent epilepsy, GGE and FE using the same covariates.

Associations between baseline metabolite concentrations and incident reported epilepsy were assessed in the full eligible UK Biobank dataset with available metabolomics measurements, including 3,418 incident reported epilepsy cases, using the same Cox regression framework and covariate adjustment as the proteomic analyses.
Bonferroni correction was applied across all 249 metabolites.
A proteomic risk score (ProRS) for incident epilepsy was constructed using Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression implemented via the glmnet R package.

LASSO simultaneously performs variable selection and coefficient regularization, making it particularly well suited for high-dimensional molecular datasets by shrinking noninformative coefficients toward zero while retaining most predictive features.
Prior to model fitting, NPX values were standardized (mean = 0, SD = 1).
The dataset was randomly divided into equally sized training and testing subsets.
Cox LASSO regression was used, adjusting for age, sex, and the first four genetic principal components (PCs).

Missing-value imputation and standardization were performed within the training data and cross-validation folds to prevent information leakage, and the optimal λ was selected using five-fold cross-validation.
The final model was refitted on the training set and applied unchanged to the independent testing set to calculate individual-level ProRS.
A metabolomic risk score (MetRS) for incident epilepsy was generated using the same analytical framework.

Standardized metabolite concentrations were used as input, the dataset was split into equally sized training and testing subsets, and the covariate-adjusted LASSO regression with five-fold cross-validation was performed to identify the optimal λ before calculating MetRS values for the independent test cohort.

To evaluate the complementary predictive value of genetic and molecular biomarkers for incident epilepsy, we systematically compared ten prediction models incorporating combinations of polygenic (PRS), proteomics (ProRS), and metabolomic (MetRS) risk scores.

Ten logistic regression models were evaluated, including a baseline model containing age, sex, and the first four genetic principal components; models including each individual risk score; baseline-adjusted models; pairwise combinations of risk scores; and a fully integrated model combining PRS, ProRS, MetRS, and demographic covariates.

text.text: To distinguish proteins that may contribute causally to epilepsy development from proteins representing downstream disease-associated biomarkers, we performed proteome-wide twosample MR using independent cis-pQTLs as genetic instruments.

Among the 2,923 proteins evaluated, 13 protein-epilepsy associations, involving 12 unique proteins, reached significance after false discovery rate (FDR) correction, indicating that only a small subset of circulating proteins showed genetic support for a potential causal role (Figure 3, Supplemental Table S3).

Consistent with the proteomic findings, prospective metabolomic profiling revealed widespread systemic alterations preceding epilepsy diagnosis.

text.text: Rather than relying on a single biomarker, the ProRS integrated 32 proteins representing multiple complementary aspects of epilepsy biology, including neuronal injury, glial activation, immune regulation, lysosomal function, cellular stress responses, and vascular biology.

NEFL contributed the largest positive coefficient in the model (weight = 0.443), consistent with its role as sensitive marker of neuroaxonal injury and its strong prospective association with incident epilepsy.

Other highly weighted proteins included RNF149 (0.234), CPVL (0.140), CTSL (0.135), and VSIG4 (0.115), implicating immune modulation, lysosomal activity, and neuroinflammatory pathways as major contributors to epilepsy risk prediction.

Additional positively weighted proteins, including GDF15, GFAP, SPINK1, and ACE2, further highlighted the contribution of cellular stress responses, astroglial activation, and epithelial defense, and vascular regulation to the prospective molecular signature.

Conversely, RAB6A (-0.211), TNR (-0.156), and NRXN3 (-0.112) were assigned negative coefficients, indicating that higher circulating levels of these proteins contributed negatively to the prediction model.

These proteins are involved in vesicle trafficking, extracellular matrix organization, and synaptic function, suggesting that preserved neuronal homeostasis may characterize individuals at lower risk of developing epilepsy.

Using prospective multi-omic profiling integrated with human genetics, we demonstrate that circulating plasma proteins and metabolites capture biological processes preceding epilepsy diagnosis and provide information complementary to inherited genetic susceptibility.

Our findings independently confirm and substantially extend the recent prospective plasma proteomic analysis by Zhang et al., 27 which similarly identified NEFL and GDF15 as the strongest circulating predictors of incident epilepsy.

text.text: Our study extends this work by integrating proteomics with metabolomics, polygenic score (PRS) prediction, MR, and Bayesian colocalization (BC) to distinguish predictive biomarkers from genetically supported molecular determinants and to evaluate their complementary value for prospective epilepsy risk stratification.
Consistent with both studies, NEFL and GDF15 emerged as biologically compelling biomarkers among the 116 proteins associated with incident epilepsy.

NEFL is a wellestablished indicator of neuroaxonal injury 46 , and has consistently been linked to seizure burden 22, 23 , drug-resistant epilepsy 24, 25 , cognitive impairment, supporting the concept that neuronal damage is already detectable during the preclinical phase of epilepsy. 26 GDF15, a stress-response cytokine induced by mitochondrial dysfunction and cellular stress, has emerged as a promising biomarker across neurological disorders 47, 48 .

text.text: Beyond these individual markers, the predominance of proteins involved in immune regulation, lysosomal biology, vascular function, and glial activation suggests that epilepsy development is accompanied by coordinated systemic biological responses well before clinical onset.
The pronounced sexspecific signatures observed in our study indicate that biological mechanisms preceding epilepsy may differ between males and females.

The proteomics risk score (ProRS), derived from only 32 proteins, represented the strongest predictor of incident epilepsy, stratifying individuals in the highest quintile into a 3.5-fold higher risk group than those in the lowest quintile.
The ProRS outperformed both the metabolomic risk score (MetRS) and the current epilepsy PRS, while integration of additional molecular layers provided only modest improvements in discrimination.
Discriminative performance was notably stronger when analyses were restricted to individuals with earlyonset (<18 years) epilepsy (AUC=0.79).

text.text: As molecular profiling in UKB occcured later in adulthood, this analysis should not be interpreted as prospective prediction of childhoodonset epilepsy.

Rather, it suggests that the combined molecular and genetic profile more strongly distinguishes individuals with a history of early-onset epilepsy, a group expected to contain a greater proportion of genetic epilepsies.
Importantly, proteomic and genetic risk contributed independently and additively, with individuals carrying both high ProRS and high PRS exhibiting the highest cumulative incidence of epilepsy.

These findings are consistent with studies from other complex diseases such as stroke, 15 Alzheimer's, 51 and cardiovascular disease 52 , where circulating protein signatures outperform polygenic risk scores for shortterm disease prediction while capturing ongoing pathophysiological processes.

text.text: The substantially higher discriminatin achieved by the ProRS compared with the PRS should not be interpreted as indicating a limited contribution of inherited susceptibility to epilepsy.

The two scores capture fundamentally different dimensions of risk; the PRS represents lifelong inhertited susceptibility, whereas circulating proteins reflect dynamic biological states at the time of sampling and may capture age-related, acquired, and prodomal processes preceding diagnosis.
The superior predictive performance of the ProRS should therefore not be interpreted as evidence that all constituent proteins are causal mediators of epilepsy.
Rather, circulating signatures likely integrate multiple downstream biological processes during the prodromal phase of disease.
Our MR analyses support this interpretation by identifying a subset of proteins with genetic evidence consistent with potential causal involvement.
Together, these complementary analyses illustrate how prospective molecular profiling and human genetics can distinguish predictive biomarkers from putative therapeutic targets.

text.text: Several limitations warrant consideration.

First, although UK Biobank (UKB) offers one of the largest prospective multi-omic data sets at population scale, the relatively small number of incident epilepsy cases limited statistical power for subtype-specific analyses.
Second, in UKB participants are predominantly of European ancestry and are affected by healthy volunteer bias, potentially limiting generalizability of our findings to other populations 71.

text.text: Third, epilepsy ascertainment relied primarily on hospital records using ICD coding and selfreported diagnoses, resulting in a heterogeneous mixture of epilepsy phenotypes, including GGE and FE together with structural, vascular, inflammatory, metabolic, and other acquired epilepsies.
Consequently, the incident epilepsy phenotype represented in UKB differs substantially from the clinically characterized cohorts used to derive current epilepsy GWAS and PRSs.
This difference in phenotype composition is likely to explain the relatively modest performance of the epilepsy PRS observed in our study.
Fourth, the UKB predominantly includes middle-aged and older adults.

Current epilepsy PRSs are primarily based on large case-control GWAS enriched for individuals with epilepsy onset during childhood, adolescence, or early adulthood, where inherited genetic susceptibility plays a particularly prominent role.

In contrast, incident epilepsy in UKB occurs at considerably older ages and includes a substantial proportion of acquired epilepsies, for which currently available epilepsy PRSs are not expected to capture fully the underlying disease risk.
This phenotype and-at-onset mismatch is likely to attenuate PRS performance in the present prospective setting.

Consistent with this interpretation, predictive performance improved markedly in participants with epilepsy onset at ≤18 years of age, a subgroup expected to contain a greater proportion of genetically determined epilepsies.
Importantly, these findings should not be interpreted as evidence against a major genetic contribution to epilepsy.

GGE is among the most heritable common neurological disorders, and the predominance of MR signals observed for GGE in our study further supports the strong influence of inherited susceptibility in this subtype.

Rather, our results suggest that circulating proteomic biomarkers capture dynamic biological processes that are shared across genetically determined and acquired epilepsies and therefore provide complementary information to inherited genetic risk in population-based cohorts.

This distinction between inherited susceptibility and dynamic disease-associated biology is likely to become increasingly important as multi-omic approaches are integrated into epilepsy risk prediction and precision medicine.

Finally, although MR and colocalization analyses strengthened causal inference for several proteins, experimental validation will be required to confirm the biological mechanisms underlying the identified associations.

In addition, independent replication in external prospective cohorts, including more diverse populations and larger numbers of clinically well-characterized epilepsy subtypes, will be essential to establish the generalizability and clinical utility of the proposed molecular risk scores.

By extending prospective plasma proteomics with metabolomics and human genetic analyses, our study demonstrates that prospective multi-omic profiling captures complementary dimensions of epilepsy biology that are not fully reflected by inherited genetic susceptibility alone.

Circulating proteomic signatures provide the strongest predictive information, metabolomic profiles reveal systemic metabolic alterations preceding disease onset, and human genetics identifies a subset of proteins with evidence supporting causal involvement in epilepsy.

Together, these findings establish a framework that combines prediction with mechanistic prioritization, advancing molecular risk stratification and potential therapeutic target discovery for epilepsy while illustrating the broader potential of prospective multiomic profiling for precision medicine in complex neurological disorders.
